Testimony Before the Committee on Appropriations and Financial Affairs in Support of L.D. 507 "An Act to Authorize a General Fund Bond Issue to Fund LifeFlight of Maine"
April 15, 2025 1:00 Public Hearing Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, and Distinguished members of the Committee on Appropriations and Financial Affairs. My name is Allison Navia. I have been an airport manager in the State of Maine for over 16 years now and I am Chair of the Maine Aeronautical Advisory Board for the Maine Department of Transportation. I have worked with LifeFlight of Maine throughout my career and their work has saved lives of people close to me. LifeFlight plays an incredibly important role in our state that goes beyond both aviation and medical care. The LifeFlight business model is time-tested, thoroughly planned, and responsible. The professionalism and expertise of their staff at every level ensure that their highly technical mission, which combines precision aviating and hospital-level care, not only functions but continuously improves and expands. The ability to fund raise and enter into public-private partnerships speaks to past impacts and future success. The organization is largely dependent on the state's aviation infrastructure, which is underfunded and often struggles to maintain existing facilities, let alone upgrade to more technologically advanced and safer systems. LifeFlight has helped many airports and hospitals improve this infrastructure, but cannot do this solely through its own funding mechanisms. This bond provides a critical piece of the financial puzzle to combine with previous bond issues, grants, and many other funding initiatives. As Chair of the Aeronautic Advisory Board to the DOT I also note improvements and additions of weather systems and fuel not only help assure the availability of LifeFlight but improve the safety of all aviation and viability of our community airports. Improving weather forecasting sources for the National Weather Service forecasts also helps all of our industries such as farming, forestry, and fishing who depend on accurate and timely weather. A bond for LifeFlight of Maine is a worthy investment for the people of our State, its visitors, businesses, and the infrastructure needed to keep them all safe. Please vote "ought to pass" on LD 507. Respectfully submitted,
Allison Navia
Airport Manager, SFM (Sanford) and IZG (Fryeburg) Chair, Maine Aeronautical Advisory Board to Maine Department of Transportation

LD 507, An Act to Authorize a General Fund Bond Issue to Fund
LifeFlight of Maine

Before the Appropriations & Financial Affairs Committee

Good afternoon, Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine and respected colleagues on the
Appropriations & Financial Affairs Committee. My name is Ann Matlack and I represent House
District 43, which includes the communities of Cushing, Thomaston, South Thomaston, St.
George and part of Owls Head. I am here today to testify in support of LD 507, An Act to
Authorize a General Fund Bond Issue to Fund LifeFlight of Maine.

As with previous LifeFlight bond issues, LD 507 will provide capital investment for projects at
various hospitals, communities and airports around Maine. LifeFlight will manage these projects so that all the proceeds from this bond go towards the public good.

I live in St. George, where we sometimes joke that fog was created in our town. Having accurate,
functioning and available weather monitoring and cameras is essential to safety and flight
decisions, as we who live along the coast know well. With this bond, 13 new Automated Weather Observing Systems (AWOS) will be installed at hospitals, on islands and at air strips. On the coast, replacement weather stations will be placed on Monhegan, Matinicus, Vinalhaven,
Stonington and Bar Harbor, and the FAA will put a new weather station at the airport in Belfast.
Additionally, the FAA will replace nine of the 16 AWOS previously installed using bonds, USDA funding and congressionally-directed spending. These systems will be located at airports
and LifeFlight will support all of the maintenance on these stations. With MEMA and now one
of the woodland companies, they have installed 35 weather cameras and are planning another 11
installations.

The bond will help with updating communication relay towers, which are also used by mutual aid helicopters from Boston MedFlight, Dartmouth Hitchcock and the military.

The bond will help rebuild nine hospital helipads.
It will allow LifeFlight to update fuel farms at major receiving hospitals and install small fuel farms at hospitals in Aroostook County. Previous bonds helped Northern Aroostook Regional Airport in Frenchville and Northern Maine Regional Airport in Presque Isle obtain fuel trucks then worked with the airports to manage the fuel. Rapid refueling saves time for patients.

District 43: Cushing, Thomaston, South Thomaston, St. George and part of Owls Head

If fully funded, this bond will help with the purchase of a second airplane so there is a backup when the current airplane is out of service for inspections and maintenance. Assuring access via the airplane is especially important to Aroostook County. It provides more all-weather capability and improves long--distance efficiency, freeing up the helicopters. It opens up distant medical centers like the Cleveland Clinic, Johns Hopkins and Philadelphia Children's Hospital to patients
in Maine needing very specialized care not available in New England. With the FAA and MDOT, LifeFlight continues to work on runways and has rebuilt runways in
Rangeley, Jackman and Eastport, and they are gradually rebuilding the entire airport in Machias.
The FAA is supporting their national demonstration project on low-altitude instrument flight
precision navigation system.
In addition to the projects anticipated by the bond, LifeFlight has worked with the FAA and
MDOT to bring other public investments into healthcare access and improving the safety of
flight.
All of these public investments help to raise private funds to support LifeFlight's helicopters, medical technologies, education and infrastructure. I urge the Committee to approve this bond issue.

10044137: Good afternoon, Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, and members of the committee. My name is Christina Dolan, and I am here today to testify in support of LD507 I live in Van Buren with my husband Rick and our 4 young children. I am here today to share with you all my family's experience with LifeFlight of Maine and how important their role is in connecting people like us from rural Maine, to the care they need. Our journey with LifeFlight of Maine began in September of 2020 when I unexpectedly went into preterm labor during a routine medical appointment with our twin boys Brian and Matthew. Only being 33 weeks with not only twins, but one twin had a known heart condition, the medical staff immediately called upon LifeFlight of Maine to transport me to Bangor for a safe delivery. Unfortunately by the time the plane arrived, I was too far advanced to safely fly. I would have to give birth in Caribou. Plans changed and the plane left to retrieve not 1 but 2 NICU teams to aid in the safe delivery and subsequent transport of my baby boys. As I was rolled into the operating room I just kept praying that the LifeFlight Team would arrive soon. Just as baby A was delivered a nurse yelled out "Don't worry Christina, LifeFlight is here." Baby A finally cried, and I did as well out of pure relief. 2 minutes later Baby B was born and gave a short cry and went blue and limp. My heart sank and I watched to my left a nurse in a green flight suit work alongside another nurse on our baby. We didn't need one transport, we needed two. So the medical team made a decision who was to go to Bangor first. Matthew our Baby B went first as he was immediately intubated and fighting for his life. They quickly rolled him into my room to say "see you later" and off he went. A few hours later they came back for Baby A, Brian and transported him to Bangor. The boys did well in the NICU and were able to come home after 26 days! Unlike many, Our story with LifeFlight doesn't end here. In March of 2021 Matthew had open heart surgery at Boston Children's Hospital. After some serious complications we finally came home in May. 5 days after being home Matthew stopped breathing in his crib. We rushed him back to the same hospital where he was born where they tried their best to stabilize him. The ER doctor knew he needed to get back to Boston. LifeFlight of Maine was called again to get our boy to the life saving medical care he needed. Again on the fixed wing he was transported to Portland to await a bed in Boston. LifeFlight of Maine has helped our family not once, but twice. Without updated infrastructure this lifesaving service is not possible. All three of these flights on the fixed wing ,we were the lucky ones. 40% of the time flights on a fixed wing don't happen due to the plane being out of service for required or unscheduled maintenance because there is only one plane. Without this service I am certain one if not both of my young boys wouldn't be here today. It's stories like ours that show the importance of LifeFlight of Maine's infrastructure and fleet. Please consider authorizing a general fund bond for LifeFlight of Maine to support those in need like Brian & Matthew who without this service, wouldn't have stood a fighting chance to live.

Good afternoon, Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, and members of the committee. My name is Dave Coughlan and I am here today to testify in support of LD507.
I am proud to say that I am a lifelong Mainer. My wife and I live in Yarmouth and we spend a lot of time in Bethei as we are avid skiers. In February of 2009 I skied all day at Sunday River on Saturday of Presidents Day weekend. I remember complaining of an earache before my ski day
had finished and also that evening. I have no recollection of falling that day but as the next
morning came a fever and nausea developed and my wife was unable to get me to respond to any questions. My condition was rapidly deteriorating and before the ambulance arrived I had slipped into a coma. The EMTs decided to transport me to Bethei Regional Airport and LifeFlight
was enroute. I was flown to CMMC in Lewiston in 15 minutes. There the medical team
discovered a hairline fracture at the base of my skull behind my right ear. After multiple rounds
of tests, I was diagnosed with bacterial meningitis and steady doses of antibiotics were
administered.
I remained in a coma for 5 days with no clear prognosis or time frame for recovery as my family and friends hoped and prayed for the best. In my 5th day in ICU I awoke from the coma and began my comeback. Overall I spent 2 weeks in the hospital on the antibiotics and once the
meningitis had been eliminated I was released to go home to continue with rehab and adjust to everyday life. I was so fortunate to emerge from this event with no physical drawbacks and I have continued to ski and bike with no restrictions. I am forever grateful to LifeFlight for saving my life since time was critical in my care. In the 16 years since my accident I have met the LifeFlight team that was involved in my transport, many of the supporting staff, and been fortunate to be up close to the helicopters and learn more about them. In 2021 when the third helicopter was added to the fleet I learned that it had new advanced medical equipment that was not yet even invented when I flew in
2009. As I often see or hear the LifeFlight helicopter in the air it always gets me thinking of that patient and the network of people involved from local emergency crews to EMT's and flight
nurses, pilots, and communications personnel in touch with hospitals to make all this work. I hope to see LD507 pass and assure that all parts of Maine be accessible for life saving care.
Thank you, Dave Coughlan

Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, and honorable members of the Committee: Thank you for the
opportunity to testify today in strong support of LD 507, legislation that proposes a $13,485,000 bond
issue to strengthen Maine's emergency medical aviation infrastructure through investments in LifeFlight
of Maine.
I offer this testimony not only as a State Representative, but as a lifelong resident of Boothbay, where the need for reliable, fast, and advanced emergency transport has only grown more urgent over the last
decade.
Twelve years ago, our region experienced a significant loss with the closure of St. Andrews Hospital in Boothbay Harbor. Since then, our nearest emergency care facility is Miles Campus at Lincoln Hospital in Damariscotta, roughly 30 minutes away--on a good day.
But in the summer months, as those of you familiar with Route 1 know, a 30-minute drive can become an hour or more. Congestion, road construction, tourists, and seasonal volume all make consistent, timely access to emergency care an uncertainty that our residents and visitors simply cannot afford-
especially in life-threatening situations like stroke, trauma, or cardiac arrest.

That's why LifeFlight of Maine is a vital part of our emergency medical system.
The investments proposed in LD 507 directly support the tools that LifeF1ight needs to keep saving
lives, especially in communities like mine, where geography and infrastructure present significant
challenges.

This bond would:

District 48: Boothbay, Boothbay Harbor, Edgecomb, South Bristol, Southport and Westpoit Island

o Provide $4.15 million to upgrade helipads at hospitals across the state--including a critical new
helipad at Lincoln Hospital Miles Campus, our region's closest emergency care center and a designated Critical Access Hospital. This upgrade is essential for ensuring that patients from the Boothbay peninsula, the Pemaquid peninsula, and our island communities can be transported quickly and safely. - Invest in fueling infrastructure to reduce mission delays, which is particularly important for rural and coastal regions. o Modemize communications and weather systems, helping to coordinate response across agencies and ensure flight safety during increasingly unpredictable Maine weather.
0 And provide for a dedicated emergency fixed-wing aircraft to serve when helicopters can't fly.
We must recognize that Lifel-`light is not a luxu1y---it is a necessity. It is the difference between life and
death in critical cases. And it is often the only timely path to advanced medical care for residents in
Boothbay, Boothbay Harbor, on Southport and Westport Islands, as well as throughout Lincoln County's coastal and island communities.
By voting to advance this bond to the voters, We give Mainers the chance to affirm a shared value: that
no matter where you live in Maine, your access to emergency care should not be a matter of luck,
distance, or the season.
On behalf of the people of Boothbay and surrounding communities, I urge you to support LD 507 and
help ensure that LifeFlight remains ready, equipped, and able to serve every corner of our state.
Thank you, and I welcome any questions you may have.
District 48: Boothbay, Boothbay Harbor, Edgecornb, South Bristol, Southport and Westport Island

April 15, 2025 Senator Rotundo, Representatives Gattine and members of the Appropriations Committee, my name is Jeffrey Austin and I am here on behalf of the Maine Hospital Association.

LD 507~An Act to Authorize a General Fund Bond issue to Fund LifeFlight of Maine

Good afternoon, Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on FinancialAffairs:
My name is Joe Kellner. i live in Windham and sen/e as the Chief Executive Officer of LifeFlight of
Maine. For overtwenty years, I have been deeply involved in emergency medical services here in
Maine and am constantly reminded about how proud we should be about the innovation and
infrastructure that allows us to minimize the adverse effects of geography on healthcare outcomes.
Today, we are before you to request your support for LD 507, which would allocate bond funding to
critical infrastructure projects that allow for the continuation of a critical promise -- if you call us,
we will be able to come for you.
LifeFlight of Maine is the states' only air medical service. Together, with our mutual aid partners in
New Hampshire and Massachusetts, we provide critical care transport services that lead the
country and the world in safety, quality, and reliability. The investments in this infrastructure over the years by the people of Maine have allowed us to give a second chance to a patient with a life-
threatening bleeding disorder, a patient who had just suffered a cardiac arrest in a rural
community, a patient with a hemorrhagic stroke, a very sick respiratory patient, another patient in a
different community having a heart attack, one that was at risk of having their ain/vay completely close that needed urgent surgical inten/ention, and another patient having a stroke. None of these patients wake up in the morning planning to need LifeFlight's services, and they found themselves
in various corners of Maine, in great rural hospitals, but needing the critical inten/entions that can
only be offered at the larger tertiary care centers. The list of patients I provided you moments ago
represent the 24-hours preceding this hearing. This is not at all atypical.
LifeFlight is projected to sen/e 4,000 patients per year by 2030. The demand for LifeFlight has increased 88% over the last ten years, and we need to continue to invest in the future. The infrastructure we invest in today will give these patients their best chance at having a "tomorrow."
This bond package will fund five critical infrastructure priorities: repairing aging helipads, replacing outdated weather reporting stations, securing our statewide air medical communications system, enhancing helicopter fueling capabilities, and adding a second airplane to ourfleet. The additional

timely, life-saving care to Mainers when they need it most.

service like ours. We have also been the fortunate recipients of grant funds to develop various
programs. While we rely on insurance revenue, that doesn't come close to meeting the need of
allowing us to promise the service to anyone regardless of their ability to pay.
- Continued -

LIFEFLIGHT OF MAINE

through the provision of care the moment we meet our patients. The aircraft and infrastructure that
surround us are merely tools that enable ourteams to perform.

10044243:
Letter of Testimony in Support of LD507: An Act to Authorize a General Fund Bond Issue to Fund LifeFlight of Maine
April 14, 2025
Dear Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee,
I am writing to express my strong support for LD507: An Act to Authorize a General Fund Bond Issue to Fund LifeFlight of Maine. From its bases in Sanford, Lewiston, and Bangor, LifeFlight operates helicopters, fixed-wing airplanes, and specialized ground ambulances, serving over 2,500 patients annually, which equates to approximately seven patients per day in every corner of the state.
Since its inception in 1998, LifeFlight has been a vital lifeline for the state's residents. As past Chief Operating Officer of a rural hospital in Northern Maine, I have seen first-hand how LifeFlight of Maine is instrumental in addressing the emergent healthcare needs of individuals residing throughout rural Maine, a region marked by geographical diversity and challenging secondary roads that become perilous during the long winter season. The organization's fleet of helicopters, fixed-wing airplanes, and specialized ground ambulances ensure timely and efficient medical transportation, often reaching remote locations that are otherwise inaccessible due to poor road conditions, remote locations, and hazardous weather. Living and vacationing in remote Maine often means long-distance transport to reach community hospital emergency departments, delaying life-sustaining intervention and treatment. LifeFlight's access to helipads and heliports allows critical emergency access, enabling rapid movement of these patients from community hospitals to tertiary care centers in Maine and beyond. This capability is essential for enhancing survivability, especially in a state where geographical and meteorological challenges can significantly impede timely medical intervention. By surmounting these obstacles, LifeFlight provides crucial critical care support, enabling patients to receive essential medical interventions promptly, regardless of Maine's demanding geography and environment.
Within community hospitals, the physicians, advanced practice providers, nurses, and administrative staff view LifeFlight as a critical component to the overall healthcare system. These individuals call on LifeFlight when managing critical patients and know that LifeFlight will come. The importance of LifeFlight can be seen when examining the impact LifeFlight has on the healthcare system in Maine. LifeFlight's aircraft fly over twice the average number of patients and operating hours per annum compared other similar regional and national providers. The organization provides comprehensive critical care support for Maine's emergency care system, ranging from interhospital transport for premature newborns, managing complex trauma patients and those requiring full cardio-pulmonary intervention. In addition to interhospital transport, LifeFlight also provides direct emergency response, supporting ground firstresponder EMS services.
LifeFlight of Maine has always prioritized safety, committing to a systems approach to build a "safety envelope" environment around patients and employees, ensuring the highest level of operational safety and reliability possible. Through this bond, LifeFlight will be positioned to assist hospitals in rebuilding helipads and establishing fuel depots, both of which will decrease flight turnaround time and increase access to critical transfers to tertiary care centers. This bond will further improve access through enhancing communication systems and weather observing systems, allowing for improved response and planning around Maine's challenging winters. This dedication to safety and excellence further underscores the importance of supporting LD507.
In conclusion, LifeFlight of Maine is an indispensable asset to the state's healthcare system. The passage of LD507 will ensure that LifeFlight can continue to provide essential services to the residents of Maine,

overcoming the unique rural geographical challenges it faces. I urge you to support this Act and secure the funding needed for LifeFlight to continue its life-saving work.
Sincerely,
Leslie KR Anderson, PT, MSB
Grant Writer, Healthcare Consultant Past Chief Operating Officer, Cary Medical Center

Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine and members of the Committee on Appropriations and Financial Affairs, my name is Lisa Harvey-McPherson RN. I am submitting testimony on behalf of Northern Light Health and our member organizations in support of this bill. Northern Light Health member organizations include 10 hospitals located in southern, central, eastern and northern Maine, 8 nursing facilities, air and ground ambulance, behavioral health, addiction treatment, pharmacy, primary and specialty care practices and a state-wide home care and hospice program. Ninety three percent of Maine's population lives in the Northern Light Health service area. Northern Light Health is also proud to be one of Maine's largest employers with more than 10,000 employees statewide.
In 1998, Maine was the only state in the country without access to dedicated medical helicopters. There was no infrastructure to support air medical operations and only two of Maine's 36 hospitals had helipads. There were no helipads at the major trauma centers, no statewide communication system to support air medical operations, no maintenance facilities, limited weather reporting, and limited fuel availability outside of major airports. To address this challenge, Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center partnered with Central Maine Medical Center providing leadership and resources as the founding organizations for LifeFlight of Maine.
To assure safe and high-quality operations LifeFlight had to build a system from scratch using lessons learned from across the world and partnerships with other highperformance providers. In the ensuing years, with private and public support, including three publicly supported bond issues, LifeFlight has built a comprehensive system to support the safe delivery of aviation medicine, incorporating an envelope of weather reporting, low-level instrument flight operations, fuel, communications, and state-ofthe-art aircraft to assure the safety of the LifeFlight teams and patients.

LD 507 An Act to Authorize a General Fund Bond Issue to Fund LifeFlight of Maine
Testimony in Support April 15, 2025
Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine and members of the Committee on Appropriations and Financial Affairs, this testimony is offered in support of LD 507. My name is Norm Dinerman, M.D. I am a founding physician member of LifeFlight of Maine and continue to serve as its Medical Director. I also serve as the founding Medical Director of the Northern Light Health Integrated Transfer Center. In my previous position, I was the Chief, Emergency Medicine Service, Eastern Maine Medical Center, from 1988 until 2006. My area of intense focus is that of patient flow, logistics and hospital resource optimization.
Since founding LifeFlight more than 25 years ago, we have sought to answer a fundamental question: "If geography is destiny, must it be determinative of health care outcome?" Our answer to this question became our mission- How do we mitigate the adverse influence of geography on health care outcome? Upon the inauguration of LifeFlight, Governor King succinctly stated: "Maine just got smaller". Beyond the ability of LifeFlight to traverse vast distances within and beyond the bucolic beauty of the state however, is not only a `promise' to our patients, but a promise to our physicians as well. This promise is to partner with every hospital, every physician, every nurse and every administrator to tether the totality of their talent, gifts of affection and expertise to that of one another. In so doing, to leverage the creativity (and resources) of the entire health care system on behalf of the patient.
We consider every transfer and transport of a patient from one hospital to another as a "physician prescriptive event". As such, LifeFlight is a physician directed `therapeutic intervention' on behalf of the most critically ill and injured patient. Fully 92% of LifeFlight transports are between hospitals. In this regard, LifeFlight is called upon to continue the life-saving interventions, frequently initiated by

EMS pre-hospital personnel, through those applied by hospital physicians and nurses, as patients are transported to tertiary care hospitals within the state, and beyond, to those institutions providing quaternary care, as needed. The manner in which LifeFlight accomplishes this is the foundation of our partnership with the entire health care system, as follows:
� LifeFlight provides on-site, shoulder to shoulder bedside support to the physician and nurse team caring for the patient at the referring hospital- Whether this be intubation of the patient, assisting with placement of chest tubes, measurement of critical laboratory values or providing an extra-set of hands to manage one or more critical patients at the same time, LifeFlight Flight Medics and Flight Nurses work side by side with hospital team members to `stabilize' a critically ill or injured patient to ready them for transport
� Enroute patient management and transport- LifeFlight team members continue the interventions undertaken at the referring hospital to maintain and advance the `stabilization' of the patient. As needed, they assertively and aggressively respond to any deterioration of the patient, should that occur
Each of the above actions by the LifeFlight team, that of on-site support and enroute management and transport, taken as a whole, provide for the `continuity of care', so desperately needed by the most vulnerable patients. It is this continuity which is as determinative of health care outcome as is the speed of transport itself and for which physicians and nurses spend their careers perfecting their practice. Without this reliable continuity of care by and between members of the health care team, the most arduous, adroit, and admirable expertise of any one physician and hospital staff is not likely to achieve the success we have experienced in this state, and certainly not over time.
This proposed bond issue placed before you speaks to the need for our state to sustain, strengthen and continue the evolution of LifeFlight. In the last analysis, we enable the gifts of our physicians,

nurses and administrative colleagues to be applied at the bedside and in the air or by ground, on behalf of the patient, from neonate to elderly adult. This partnership enables the most contemporary practice of medicine to extend to the farthest reaches of Maine and in politically ecumenical fashion. In so doing, we are mitigating the `adverse influence' of the distance between hospital team members, to provide another chance at patient survival and productivity.
The question we ask of ourselves at the end of each day, and patient by patient, is: "Were we worthy of the trust". This question extends not only to our patients and the medical professionals who entrust them to our care, but also to the larger society of Maine citizens and their legislative representatives who have allocated scarce financial resources to build our system. In this regard, we remain ever-mindful of the need to optimize a `return on investment'. Each resource acquisition of LifeFlight, be it for personnel, training equipment, transport assets or infrastructure, is pursued with deliberate regard for this concept and tested against its affordability in the context of acknowledged economic constraints. This bond issue for which this testimony is a part reflects the fiduciary duty to which we hold ourselves, no less than to you, our legislative colleagues.
I do hope that this physician perspective will take its place beside additional testimony offered to you, in enthusiastic support of LifeFlight's request for funding by way of LD 507. We fully appreciate the complex, intense and daunting task which lawmakers face in apportioning precious funds. We hope that LifeFlight remains worthy of your trust and stand before you in trust of your judgement as to the value and `return on investment' of this fiscal request.
Respectfully,
Norm Dinerman, M.D. FACEP

services. LD507: An Act to Authorize a General Fund Bond Issue to Fund LifeFlight of Maine
LifeFlight is proposing to work with the legislature to enact a bond to fund critically needed aviation infrastructure. Through public private partnerships, LifeFlight has built a first in the nation comprehensive low altitude aviation infrastructure to assure the highest levels of safety
and reliability for LifeFlight to be there when needed.
Bacl<ground LifeFlight is a unique nonprofit, the only healthcare entity serving every Maine community and hospital. Working from bases in Sanford, Lewiston, and Bangor using helicopters, fixed wing airplanes, and specialized ground ambulances LifeFlight serves over 2,500 patients per annum, around seven patients per day in every corner of Maine.
ln 1998, Maine was the only state in the country without access to medical helicopters. In addition to being economically challenged and one of the most rural states by population density, Maine has the most complex and hostile aviation weather of any state other than Alaska. Extremes of temperature, dense forests, coastal and inland mountains, the Labrador current (fog), and a service area of over 40,000 square miles including hundreds of islands are combined challenges to 24/365 operations.
As compared regionally and nationally, LifeFlight aircraft fly over twice the average number of patients and operating hours per annum. LifeFlight provides comprehensive critical care support for Maine's emergency care system ranging from interhospital transport for premature newborns to the complex patients on full cardio-pulmonary bypass. In addition to LifeFlight's role in supporting emergency interhospital transport, LifeFlight provides direct response to emergency scenes supporting ground EMS services. l.ifeFlight responds to remote areas and islands, major multipatient events such as the Lewiston shooting, and supplies critical personnel and equipment to hospitals during major
events.
